CNBC reported that during a recent all-hands, OpenAI, CFO, Sarah Fryer told staff that ARR annualized recurring revenue for July had exceeded the entire second quarter, adding and Q2 was no slouch. Now without the full context, it is not exactly clear what Fryer meant and the articles didn't do a lot to clear that up, but the takeaway certainly was that OpenAI had an absolute pananza of a month. Then on Thursday, Axios reported that Anthropic was also seeing revenue skyrocket. Indeed, back of the napkin math put Anthropic at a $71 billion run rate, up from $47 billion in May when they last discussed revenue. This figure was based on a post from Tay Kim, who was referencing data from AI Investment Research Platform Funda.

Meanwhile, their data also showed that OpenAI was sitting just shy of $50 billion in ARR. Now, obviously, this data should be treated as a very rough estimate, but it seems directionally correct based on Fryer's comments. It also lines up with estimates from semi-analysis, who at the beginning of the month, wrote that Anthropic is currently operating above $60 billion in ARR, and looks at to end the quarter with $1 billion in profit. And some believe they will just keep going. In a recent blog post, Dwarkesh Patel wrote, Anthropic likely ends the year with $100-150 billion in revenue. Now, in the one hand, those numbers seem absolutely gobsmacking, but if Anthropic really jumped $10 billion in ARR in July alone, it doesn't seem impossible. Pointing out that Dwarkesh is in a position to have a lot of behind-the-scenes conversations, former Atlantic author Derek Thompson noted that if Anthropic can hit this mark, they will have eclipsed the revenue-generating capacity of Tesla and SpaceX combined.

My position on that is pretty clear. However, very importantly, it is very easy for any of us who intersect primarily with one part or one theme of the market to think that that's the most important thing in markets. However, if you take a quick peek outside of the AI ecosystem, you'll notice that a lot of the bearer sentiment on AI right now has absolutely nothing to do with AI fundamentals. This week, the Federal Reserve declined to raise interest rates, but many analysts now believe a rate hike is coming as soon as inflation picks up. The ongoing fracas of the Iran War is making investors extremely jittery, and from the beginning of the year where we saw macro conditions ripe for a boom in speculative text stocks, over the past couple of months the market has transitioned into a decidedly risk off mood. It is important for us to be able to distinguish when AI-related market prices going down has to do with some change in belief about AI or whether they are just the biggest stocks being influenced by broader concerns.

That's around 3.4% of the adult population. As many as 360,000 accounts were liquidated, meaning they were forced to sell after failing to meet a margin-called. It's always dangerous to try to say market moves are only about this thing versus that thing, and right now you're seeing a competition for interpretations around these particular moves. To sum, it's a notoriously cyclical semiconductor industry experiencing a predictable crash as long-term AI demand is questioned, but on the other hand, there is a very mechanical story playing out, as a sizable chunk of the Korean population is forced to sell into a price crash. Those two interpretations have wildly different implications for what this all says about the state of AI markets in general. Another big story doing the rounds with AI bears is the problem of off-balance sheet debt. As I've been discussing for months, we're at the phase where the hyper-scalers are increasingly having to turn away from funding the infrastructure bill that themselves, towards instead turning to debt to fund that billed out.

In his fantastic newsletter notes on the crisis, Nathan Tankus wrote an extremely detailed comparison between hidden data center debt and the CDOs that brought the financial system to its knees in 2008. And in this particular instance, I do think it is worth noting the source. Nathan is not a David Zack Silicon Valley venture capitalist talking his own book. He's an extremely left-leaning, extremely earnest markets commentator who's been writing this newsletter since COVID, who if you have watched for the last five years or so as I have, is basically temperamentally incapable of making an argument that isn't just based on the best information that he can find, regardless of whose talking points it reinforces. In any case, when it comes to this comparison between hidden data center debt and collateralized debt obligations, Nathan's core argument is that the hyperscalers are fundamentally a different type of borrower to the subprime borrowers during the financial crisis.

Now, the great challenge for all of these companies continues to be how to get very short-term investors on-site enough to be able to continue to do what you need to do for the long-term while also not making too many concessions to what you need in the long-term to compete. Rounding out the week was Amazon who reported strong earnings in a slight CapEx bump. AWS sales are up 37% year-over-year, and that seems good enough for investors to endorse this year's CapEx forecast rising from 200 billion to 220 billion. CEO Andy Jassy explained the increase as increased costs, rather than expanded scope, but he also defended the spending as clearly necessary. Jassy said, even at that amount, we will still not have enough capacity to meet all the demand we have in 2026, and I believe this dynamic will also be true in 2027. In fact, the demand we already have for 2028 is striking, and this, again, friends, is why the acceleration of revenue for Anthropic and OpenAI matters so much.

Among other effects, it gives the hyperscalers the latitude they need to hike spending to match rising costs and keep the AI trade rolling. The hyperscalers say the demand is still there and it's still rising, which brings us to perhaps the wildest story of the week. Tech earnings quickly took a backseat as the most famous AI hedge fund blew up. On Friday morning, it was reported that Leopold Ashen Brenner's fund, situational awareness, had been liquidated and taken over by Citadel. Matt Leopold has had a crazy story. He, like me, was a refugee of FTX madness, and he, like me, found his way into AI, although intersecting with the industry in a very different spot. While he was originally at OpenAI, he left under some cloud of questions around whether it was disagreements in policy or him speaking too freely about internal matters, but where his story really picked up steam was the summer of 2024, when he dropped that namesake SA situational awareness, a 165-page tone that woke many on Wall Street up to how fundamentally powerful AI would likely change the world.

Now in terms of what happens next, the ultimate buyer of the situational awareness portfolio Citadel is rumored to have gotten a 20% to 50% discount on the positions. That means there's not really a huge rush to sell it into the market. Now no fund in the world has the ability to hold $120 billion in exposure indefinitely, but Citadel is certainly among the best place to sell it off slowly. Citadel also isn't a directional player. They make money by trading often and always try to maintain a neutral market position. That means that they were naturally hedged against this drawdown and likely aren't in the same vulnerable position a situational awareness was. Now it is also worth contrasting this blow up with other famous hedge fund failures. When LTCM collapsed in 1994, they were trading currency and bonds on massive leverage. The reason that metastasized into the Asian financial crisis was not because a hedge fund blew up, but because the currency market couldn't absorb their liquidation.

You may not be interested in politics, but politics is interested in you. That's kind of how I feel about AI markets for many of us who are here around the AI daily brief. Certainly some of you are professional investors, for whom this is all obviously very mission critical and important. But for the average folks who are just trying to understand how AI is going to affect them, my argument is that at this point, AI is so integrally tied to so many parts of the economy, and so much of the current structure of the economy, that even if you are not primarily an investor, it is worth understanding what's going on. And right now, if we have to sum this all up, this story is one continued concerns around circular financing and just the nature of the debt in general behind the AI buildout, which as I've said in the past, are some of the best pressure release valves when it comes to whether an AI bubble would fully form. A very notable hedge fund that blew up, not mostly because of AI fundamentals, but instead because of tried and true issues of leverage. But behind it all, a demand story for AI, which does nothing but continue to grow. Hopefully you feel like you have a better sense of what's going on out there now, for now that's going to do it for today's AI Daily Brief. I appreciate you listening or watching as always, and until next time, peace.

card.summary_hint: ## Description MIT 6.034 Artificial Intelligence, Fall 2010 View the complete course: http://ocw.mit.edu/6-034F10 Instructor: Patrick Winston We consider a block-stacking program, which can answer questions about its own behavior, and then identify an animal given a list of its characteristics.  Finally, we discuss how to extract knowledge from an expert, using the example of bagging groceries. License: Creative Commons BY-NC-SA More information at http://ocw.mit.edu/terms More courses at http://ocw.mit.edu ## Tags system diagram, subroutine, trace, behavior, heuristics, knowledge…

clips.text: They're all written in Java, principally because I can therefore make them available to you and to the rest of the world by way of Web Start. A few weeks ago, I was mucking around with the system and broke the version on the server, and within 15 minutes, I got an email from somebody in the depths of Anatolia complaining about it and asking me to bring it back up. This particular program is patterned after an early AI classic. And it was the business end of a program written by Terry Winograd, who became, and is, a professor of computer science at Stanford University-- which is on the west coast for those of you-- on the strength of his work on the natural language front end of this program.

Have you ever written a program that's answered questions about its own behavior? Probably not. Would you like to learn how to do that? So by the end of the hour, you'll be able to write this program and many more like it that know how to answer questions about their own behavior. There have been tens of thousands of such programs written, but only by people who know the stuff I'm going to tell you about right now, OK? So what I want to do is I want to start by taking this program apart on the board and talking to you about the modules, the subroutines that it contains. So here it is. The first thing we need to think about, here are some blocks. What has to happen if I'm going to put the bottom block on the larger block?

How does it answer a how question? Sebastian? SEBASTIAN: It goes down one level. PROFESSOR PATRICK WINSTON: You go down one level. So you start off all the way up here with a put-on. You will say, oh, well I did these four things. You say, why did you grasp B1? It will say because I was trying to clear its top. Why did you clear its top? Because I was trying to get rid of it. Why were you trying to get rid of it? Because I was trying to put it on the table. So that's how it answers how questions, by going down in this tree and this trace of the program of action so as to see how things are put together. What are these things that are being put together? What's the word I've been avoiding so as to bring this to a crescendo? What are these objectives, these things it wants to do?

For example, I could say, why did you put B6 on B3? Because you told me to. All right, so the complexity of the behavior is largely a consequence not of the complexity of the program in this particular case, but the building of this giant goal tree as a consequence of the complexity of the problem. This brings us to one of our previous matters-- early on to one of the gold star ideas of today. And this gold star idea goes back to a lecture given in the late '60s by Herb Simon, who was the first Nobel Laureate in the pseudo Nobel Prize for economics. Is that right, Bob? Was he the first? All right, he was the first winner of the Nobel Prize, pseudo Nobel Prize in economics.

Several rules, R1, R2-- and there needs to be an and gate here-- that's R3 and an R4. All of which indicate that this animal is a cheetah. So we built ourself a little rule-based expert system that can recognize exactly one animal, but you could imagine filling out this system with other rules so that you could recognize giraffes and penguins and all the other sorts of things you find in a small zoo. So when you have a system like this that works as I've indicated, then what we're going to call that, we're going to give that a special name, and we're going to call that a forward-chaining rule-based-- because it uses rules-- expert system.

So look at this. If I say to it, why were you interested in the animal's claws? Because I was trying to see if it was a carnivore. How did you know that the animal is a mammal? Because it has hair. Why did you think it was a cheetah? Because it's a mammal, a carnivore, has spots, and very fast. So by working forward and backward in this goal tree, this too can answer questions about its own behavior. So now you know how, going forward, you can write programs that answer questions about their behavior. Either you write the subroutines so that each one is wrapped around a goal, so you've got goal-centered programming, or you build a so-called expert system using rules, in which case it's easy to make it leave behind a trace of a goal tree, which makes it possible to answer questions about its own behavior, just as this [INAUDIBLE] program did.

That's because it's working with facts to produce new facts. When you have a deduction system, you can never take anything away. But these rule-based systems are also used in another mode, where it's possible to take something away. See, in fact world, in deduction world, you're talking about proving things. And once you prove something is true, it can't be false. If it is, you've got a contradiction in your system. But if you think of this as a programming language, if you think of using rules as a programming language, then you can think of arranging it so these rules add or subtract from the database. Let me show you an example of a couple of systems. First of all, since I've talked about the MYCIN system, let me show you an example of a MYCIN dialogue.

SPEAKER 7: So no squishies on the bottom. So if you have-- PROFESSOR PATRICK WINSTON: No squishies on the bottom. SPEAKER 7: If you have tomatoes-- PROFESSOR PATRICK WINSTON: That's good. Tomatoes. SPEAKER 7: You don't want them to get squished. PROFESSOR PATRICK WINSTON: Now, there's a very different thing about squishies and tomatoes because tomato is specific, and squishy isn't. Now, one tendency of MIT students, of course, is that we all tend to generalize. I once knew a professor in the Sloan School who seemed real smart. And-- PROFESSOR PATRICK WINSTON: Then I figured out what he did. If I were to say, I'm thinking about a red apple. They'd sit back and say, oh, I see you're contemplating colored fruit today. They're just taking it up one level of abstraction. Not a genius.

You're saying to yourself, well, let's look at some specific cases. Well, what are the vocabulary items here that tell me why this problem is different from that problem? Oh, this is a cylinder instead of a sphere. Or you're working with a problem set, and you discover you can't work with the problem, and you need to get another chunk of knowledge that makes it possible for you to do it. So this sort of thing, which you think of primarily as a mechanism, heuristics for doing knowledge engineering, are also mechanisms for making yourself smarter. So that concludes what I want to talk with you about today. But the bottom line is, that if you build a rule-based expert system, it can answer questions If you build a program that's centered on goals, it can answer questions about its own behavior.

But there's one thing that's well-illustrated by our particular capturing of Hamlet here. And that is that you'll note that the ratio of gray stuff to white stuff is considerable. The gray stuff is stuff that has been deduced by rules. And the reason there's so much gray stuff in this Hamlet story is because everybody's related to everybody else. So when you kill anybody, you irritate everybody else. So look at that. A few white things, those are the things that are explicit in the story, and lots of gray stuff. So what this is suggesting is that when we tell a story, it's mostly a matter of controlled hallucination. I know what rules are in your head, so I could take advantage of that in telling the story and not have to tell you anything I'm sure you're going to know. And so that's why, we've discovered, that storytelling is largely a matter of just controlling how you're going along, a kind of controlled hallucination.

clips.text: Why is it important for Nvidia to release open models when Nvidia also sells GPUs to Frontier Labs that also release proprietary models? Why is it so important for you to keep pushing the envelope to release bigger and bigger models to train and to give away everything including the data, the training recipes, and kind of the teacher models? Why so? Tell us. >> I think that what I would say, what I've heard said a lot from from people like Jensen and Bryan Catanzaro, right? Jensen obviously leader of Nvidia, Bryan Catanzaro who heads up our research arm for Nvidia. I mean, it's integral, it's crucial to Nvidia's mission to be good at producing models because people use GPUs to make models. That's just a fact. They use them to train models, to inference with models, they use them to run their agents. And if we don't know how to build a good model, if we can't build a good model, we can't know what the best GPU is, right? We can't understand the exact best way to produce hardware. And this is a process that I think Jensen's talked a lot about up on various stages called extreme co-design, right? Where you have to kind of build the hardware with the technology at the same time. And if you just do one in a vacuum, it doesn't mean anything. And the reason we want to open it is because we think that AI is a very useful tool. And everyone should have AI and many different countries should have AI and many different organizations should have AI and they should have a blueprint we know works and is battle-tested that that you can take and you can build your own models and for your own agents. And if we're not releasing that stuff because we're doing it, so it's like if we're doing it, we may as well release it. Share the learnings and I think, you know, Bryan says this a lot like the ecosystem benefits when we release something because then the ecosystem does something with with our stuff and we learn from it and then we get better and then we make better hardware and then we make better models. That's just summarize the thoughts of people that are at the helm. That's why we do it. >> [music]

card.summary_hint: ## Hook Analysis <!-- HOOK_START --> <!-- HOOK_END --> ## Description Lilian Weng shared today that she is leaving Thinking Machines Lab to focus on her health.  I went back to this 2019 talk at OpenAI. In front of 100+ women in tech, she made a difficult frontier problem, teaching a robotic hand dexterous manipulation through reinforcement https://t.co/5H7jwtQkk7 ## Tags No tags ## Transcript [00:00:01] 太棒了，酷。 [00:00:03] 今天，我要谈谈一些研究项目 [00:00:06] 与OpenAI机器人团队的合作。 [00:00:11] 我们机器人团队的一个大问题是开发 [00:00:15] 驱动通用机器人的算法。 [00:00:18] 想想我们人类如何生活在这个世界上， [00:00:23] 我们可以烹饪、搬运物品、使用不同的工具 [00:00:30] 添加更多物品。…

clips.text: 太棒了，酷。 今天，我要谈谈一些研究项目 与OpenAI机器人团队的合作。 我们机器人团队的一个大问题是开发 驱动通用机器人的算法。 想想我们人类如何生活在这个世界上， 我们可以烹饪、搬运物品、使用不同的工具 添加更多物品。 我们充分利用身体，尤其是双手 来完成各种任务。 在某种程度上，我们就是通用机器人，对吧？ 也就是说，我们将同样的标准应用于 对这类事物的定义。 通用机器人应该能够与 现实世界非常复杂的环境进行交互 并能操控周围的各种物体。 然而，不幸的是，如今大多数面向消费者的机器人 要么只是玩具，要么非常实验性 或者专注于特定功能， 比如工厂机械臂或医疗机器人。 它们能与环境和操作工具互动， 但实际由人类操控，人类控制 每一个动作，或者它们只是回放 预设的轨迹。 它们并不真正理解环境， 也无法自主移动。 在我们的项目中，我们朝着这个目标迈出了一小步， 尝试教一个类人机器人手 通过移动物体进行手内操作。

这是一个六面体块，上面有OpenAI字样， 将其移动到目标方向。 我们认为这是一个重要问题，因为类人 机械手，这是全球性的努力。 想象一下，如果我们能很好地控制它，就有可能 自动化许多目前由人类完成的任务。 不幸的是，进展不大 在类人机械手方面，由于其复杂性 这样的系统。 为什么困难？ 首先，系统具有非常高的维度。 例如，在我们的机器人中，正如你所见 这个很酷的插图。 Shadow灵巧手有24个关节和20个执行器。 任务尤其困难，因为在操作过程中， 很多观测被遮挡且可能带有噪声。 例如，你的传感器读数可能出错 并且传感器读数可能被物体本身阻挡。 此外，几乎不可能模拟 你的物理世界100%正确。 我们解决这个问题的方法 是使用强化学习。 我们相信这是一个很好的学习方法 来控制机器人，因为我们看到了巨大进步 和巨大成功在许多应用中 通过强化学习。 你听说过OpenAI Five，AlphaGo的故事 看到强化学习不仅能与这个虚拟世界互动 还能对我们的物理现实产生影响，将非常令人兴奋。 强化学习模型有一个很大的缺点。 总的来说，如今大多数模型

数据效率不高。 你需要大量的训练样本才能 训练出一个好的模型。 一个可能的解决方案是建造一个机器人农场。 你只需并行收集数百 上千个机器人的数据，但想象一下，机器人 可能有多脆弱。 建造和维护成本非常高。 如果你想到另一个问题，一个新问题， 或者你想使用新的机器人， 很难做出改变。 此外，你的数据可能很快失效 因为机器人状态的微小变化。 因此，我们决定采用 sim2real 方法， 即每次模拟都训练模型， 但部署在实体机器人上。 这里展示我们如何控制手部模拟。 手将物体移动到目标方向。 目标显示在右侧，每当手 达到目标后，我们只需采样一个新目标。 它一直这样做，我们限制成功次数 最多50次。 这是我们的物理设置。 所有设备都安装在这个巨大的金属笼子里。 它大约这么大。 手部安装在中间。 周围环绕着动作捕捉系统。 这实际上是人们用于拍摄特效电影的系统 就像演员身上有标记点 有点类似。 这个系统追踪五个指尖的位置 在三维空间中。 我们还有三个高分辨率摄像头用于捕捉 图像作为视觉模型的输入。 我们的视觉模型预测位置方向

块。 然而，我们的模拟到现实方法 可能会严重失败，因为有很多模型 差异存在于模拟和现实之间。 如果你的模型都参考模拟环境， 真实机器人表现可能非常差。 为了解决这个问题，我们决定采用， 我们使用强化学习。 我们训练所有模拟，以便生成 技术上、理论上无限量的数据。 为了克服模拟与现实的差异， 我们使用域随机化。 域随机化指的是在模拟中随机化 不同元素，使你的策略 能够接触到各种场景 并学会如何适应。 最终，我们扩展策略使其能够适应 物理现实。 回到这一点，这个想法相对较新。 我认为他们最初在2016年提出。 研究人员尝试训练模型控制无人机 比如飞越家具或室内场景。 他们随机化了墙壁的颜色和纹理 以及家具，且未使用任何真实图像， 它们表明它在现实中表现相当不错。 在OpenAI，我们使用相同的方法来训练更好的模型 以保护物体的位置方向。 如你所见，有些随机化看起来完全 不现实，但不知何故，当我们向模型输入真实图像时，它工作得很好。 后来，我们还展示了你可以随机化 模拟中的所有物理动力学，而这个机器人 模拟中的所有物理动力学以及这个机器人 经过域随机化训练的模型效果更好 比没有的好。 我们来看看结果。 好的。

好的。 我要点击... （低节奏音乐） 你在第一个目标上确实有点吃力。 好的，没问题。 （铃声） 叮的一声表示一次成功。 这个视频会一直播放到目标50次，所以非常， 非常长，但我个人觉得看着它很舒缓， 我很喜欢。 （铃声） 我想这就够了。 这是我们完整的训练设置，在盒子A中， 我们并行生成大量环境， 在其中随机化物理动力学 和视觉外观。 基于这些，我们独立训练两个模型。 一个是策略模型，它接收指尖位置 和物体姿态以及目标，并输出 手的期望关节位置，以便 我们可以控制手。 另一个模型是视觉模型，它接收三张图像 来自不同摄像机角度，并输出物体的 位置和方向。 当我们将它部署到现实世界时，我们将 基于真实图像的视觉预测与 运动捕捉系统追踪的指尖位置相结合， 并将其输入到我们的策略控制模型中。 并输出动作，这样我们只需将其发送到真实 机器人，一切就开始移动 就像电影中展示的那样。 当我们训练策略控制模型时，

我们随机化了各种物理参数 在模拟器中，例如质量、摩擦系数、 电机增益、阻尼因子以及噪声 作用于动作和观测上。 对于修订模型，我们随机化了相机位置， 光照、材质、纹理、颜色等等， 结果效果很好。 关于我们的模型架构， 我快速过一下。 策略是一个简单的循环单元。 包含一个全连接层和LSTM。 视觉模型是直接的多相机设置。 所有三个摄像头共享这个RestNet堆栈，随后 是空间softmax。 我们的训练框架是分布式同步PBO， 近端策略优化模型。 实际上，这与训练OpenAI Five 所用的框架相同。 我们的设置每小时可生成约两年模拟 经验，相当于17,000 实体机器人，所以巨大的机器人工厂 和模拟非常棒。 当我们在现实中部署模型时，我们注意到 机器人学到的一些策略，比如手指旋转、 滑动、手指步态。 这些也是人类常用的策略， 有趣的是，我们从未明确 告诉它这些词语或鼓励这些策略。 它们会自主出现。 我们来看一些数据。 为了比较不同版本的模型，

我们将模型部署到真实机器人上，并统计 策略在掉落方块或超时前能成功多少次，最多50次。 我们首先尝试部署一个 完全没有随机化的模型。 完全没有随机化。 它在模拟中表现完美，但你看， 实际成功率中位数为零。 在真实机器人上表现极差。 然后我们加入了域随机化。 策略变得好多了， 因为成功率中位数达到13，最高50。 然后我们在视觉模型中用RGB摄像头 来追踪物体。 性能仅略有下降，仍然很好。 最后一个，我觉得这个很有趣，因为…… 我刚才提到我们的策略是循环 单元，比如LSTM，它有内部记忆。 有趣的是，看看这个记忆有多重要 所以我们用FIFO或NAS替换了这个LSTM策略 并将其部署在机器人上，性能下降 了很多，这表明记忆起着重要作用 在模拟到现实的迁移中。 策略可能利用记忆 并尝试学习如何适应。 然而，在随机化环境中训练 确实需要付出代价。 这里我们绘制了模拟中的成功次数 作为以年计量的模拟体验的函数。 如果你完全不应用随机化， 模型可以学会达到40次成功 大约需要三年的模拟
经验，但要达到同样的数字， 比如在完全随机化的环境中成功40次 则需要100年。 好的，快速总结一下，我们已经证明这种方法， 强化学习加训练模拟再加领域 随机化，在真实机器人上有效 我们希望能推动它向前发展。 非常感谢。 （观众鼓掌） 是的。 好，下一位是克里斯汀。 - 谢谢。
